idiom_name: System.Threading.Channels Channel<Order> (or a broker destination per message type)
implementation_notes: System.Threading.Channels in the BCL is a typed channel: Channel.CreateBounded<Order>(capacity) hands out a Writer/Reader pair whose element type is the channel contract, so a consumer that awaits ReadAllAsync() on the order channel can never observe an invoice, and the completion protocol (writer.Complete(), reader completion) replaces the classic 'close the channel' convention. Choose System.Collections.Concurrent.BlockingCollection<T> when the consumer is an ordinary synchronous thread and Add/Take is all you need; choose a broker destination per message type when the channel must cross a process boundary. The distributed form is explicit in .NET messaging stacks: MassTransit's topology derives the exchange/topic name from the message type and binds each consumer's queue to it, so message type and destination stay one decision rather than two.
pitfalls: A bounded channel applies backpressure through WriteAsync; using TryWrite in a loop silently drops or throws depending on FullMode, so pick Wait and let the writer await when loss is unacceptable.
Completing the writer is the only way a reader's await foreach terminates - forgetting Complete() leaves consumers awaiting forever with no exception to alert on.
Channel<T> is in-process only; handing the same Channel instance to code that must run in another process is impossible, so the distributed case needs per-message-type broker destinations instead.

variants.name: Broker destination named after the message type (MassTransit topology)
variants.idiom_name: MassTransit/Service Bus destination per message type
variants.implementation_notes: For channels that cross process boundaries the binding moves into the broker: the message type names the exchange/topic and each consumer owns a queue bound to it, so the type is the routing decision and the consumer's deserializer knows the contract without reading a header. MassTransit derives these names from the message type by default and lets you override them per message (SetEntityName, IEntityNameFormatter), which is the single source of truth this pattern needs; keep the name stable, because renaming it silently creates a second destination that nothing consumes. The trade-off against the in-process channel is operational weight: broker resources, bindings, retry and dead-letter configuration per message type instead of a single object in memory.
pitfalls: Renaming a message type or its entity name silently creates a new destination; producers keep publishing while the old queue starves.
Consumer queues bound to a shared base exchange can receive types they cannot deserialize - keep publish topology per concrete message type, and exclude base types where needed.
